input:
@here quick writeup on yesterdays outage in the payments api.

what happend: around 2:10pm the payments-api pods started crashlooping after we rolled out v4.12. the new config loader was expecting a env var called `LEDGER_URL` but the helm chart still had the old name `LEDGER_ENDPOINT`, so every pod fail on startup. because the readiness probe was passing for few seconds before the crash, the rollout didnt stop automatically and all 6 replicas was replaced.

impact: checkout was down for about 38 minutes. roughly 1,400 orders failed and customers seen a generic error page. no data was lost, the failed orders were never charged.

how we fixed it: <@U05KLM321> rolled back to v4.11 at 2:48pm and checkout recovered within two minutes. we then patched the chart and redeployed v4.12 at 4:30pm with out issues.

the error from the logs was:
```
FATAL config: required variable LEDGER_URL is not set
```

follow ups:
- make the readiness probe check the config loader, not just the http port (owner: @Nina Patel)
- add a CI check that compares env vars in code vs the helm chart
- write a runbook for rolling back payments-api, its currently only in someones head

full timeline is in the doc https://example.com/incidents/2026-10-23 , please add anything i missed. we will discuss in #incident-review on monday.
expected:
@here Below is a quick write-up of yesterday's outage in the payments API.

What happened: Around 2:10 PM, the payments-api pods started crash-looping after we rolled out v4.12. The new config loader expected an environment variable called `LEDGER_URL`, but the Helm chart still used the old name, `LEDGER_ENDPOINT`, so every pod failed on startup. Because the readiness probe passed for a few seconds before each crash, the rollout didn't stop automatically, and all 6 replicas were replaced.

Impact: Checkout was down for about 38 minutes. Roughly 1,400 orders failed, and customers saw a generic error page. No data was lost, and the failed orders were never charged.

How we fixed it: <@U05KLM321> rolled back to v4.11 at 2:48 PM, and checkout recovered within two minutes. We then patched the chart and redeployed v4.12 at 4:30 PM without issues.

The error from the logs was:
```
FATAL config: required variable LEDGER_URL is not set
```

Follow-ups:
- Make the readiness probe check the config loader, not just the HTTP port (owner: @Nina Patel)
- Add a CI check that compares the environment variables in the code with those in the Helm chart
- Write a runbook for rolling back payments-api, since it currently exists only in someone's head

The full timeline is in the doc: https://example.com/incidents/2026-10-23. Please add anything I missed. We will discuss it in #incident-review on Monday.

input:
Hey team, i want to propose that we move our nightly reports from the old cron server to the scheduler in Fernhill. right now the cron box is a single VM that nobody really owns, it runs 23 jobs and when it goes down (which happened twice last month) we only find out when someone from finance complain that there report is missing.

Fernhill already give us retries, alerting and a UI to see job history, so we would get all of that for free. the jobs themself dont need to change much, most of them are just python scripts that read from the warehouse and write a CSV to the shared bucket.

rough plan:
- week 1: inventory all 23 jobs, figure out which ones are still used and delete the dead ones
- week 2: port the 10 most critical jobs and run them in parallel with cron for a few days
- week 3: port the rest, switch off cron and decomission the VM

the main risk is that some jobs depends on files that only exist on the cron box. i found at least two that read from `/opt/reports/lookup.csv` which isnt in any repo. we will need to move those into the bucket first.

cost wise this should save around $180 a month from the VM, and Fernhill is already payed for.

@Owen Brooks you own the finance reports so i would love your input before we start. if nobody have objections i will create the tickets on thursday and share them in #data-platform.
expected:
Hey team, I'd like to propose that we move our nightly reports from the old cron server to the scheduler in Fernhill. Right now, the cron box is a single VM that nobody really owns. It runs 23 jobs, and when it goes down (which happened twice last month), we only find out when someone from finance complains that their report is missing.

Fernhill already gives us retries, alerting and a UI for viewing job history, so we would get all of that for free. The jobs themselves don't need to change much. Most of them are just Python scripts that read from the warehouse and write a CSV to the shared bucket.

Rough plan:
- Week 1: Inventory all 23 jobs, figure out which ones are still used and delete the dead ones
- Week 2: Port the 10 most critical jobs and run them in parallel with cron for a few days
- Week 3: Port the rest, switch off cron and decommission the VM

The main risk is that some jobs depend on files that only exist on the cron box. I found at least two that read from `/opt/reports/lookup.csv`, which isn't in any repo. We will need to move those files into the bucket first.

Cost-wise, this should save around $180 a month on the VM, and Fernhill is already paid for.

@Owen Brooks, you own the finance reports, so I would love your input before we start. If nobody has objections, I will create the tickets on Thursday and share them in #data-platform.

input:
Hi all, starting next monday we are changing how code reviews work in the platform team. this came out of the last two retros where alot of people said reviews are taking too long and its not clear who is suppose to review what.

what is changing:
- every PR now needs one approval from a code owner instead of two approvals from anyone. the CODEOWNERS file is already updated in the repo
- reviewers should respond within one working day. respond dont mean approve, a quick comment saying you will look tomorrow is fine
- PRs over 400 lines will get a warning label from the bot. its not a hard block but please try to split them, big PRs is the main reason reviews stall
- we are turning on the auto-assign so you no longer need to pick reviewers manually

what is not changing:
- CI still need to pass before merge
- security sensitive changes (anything under `auth/` or `billing/`) still need a second review from the security group

we will try this for six weeks and then look at the numbers. right now the median time to first review is 26 hours, the goal is to get it under 8. i will post the weekly stats in #platform-eng every friday so everyone can see how its going.

if you think something in this plan wont work for your area, reply in the thread or DM me before friday. i rather adjust it now then after people get used to it.

thanks to @Grace Liu and <@U08STU987> for helping put this together.
expected:
Hi all, starting next Monday, we are changing how code reviews work on the platform team. This came out of the last two retros, where a lot of people said reviews take too long and that it's not clear who is supposed to review what.

What is changing:
- Every PR now needs one approval from a code owner instead of two approvals from anyone. The CODEOWNERS file has already been updated in the repo
- Reviewers should respond within one working day. Responding doesn't mean approving; a quick comment saying you will look at it tomorrow is fine
- PRs over 400 lines will get a warning label from the bot. It's not a hard block, but please try to split them, since big PRs are the main reason reviews stall
- We are turning on auto-assign, so you no longer need to pick reviewers manually

What is not changing:
- CI still needs to pass before merge
- Security-sensitive changes (anything under `auth/` or `billing/`) still need a second review from the security group

We will try this for six weeks and then look at the numbers. Right now, the median time to first review is 26 hours, and the goal is to get it under 8. I will post the weekly stats in #platform-eng every Friday so everyone can see how it's going.

If you think something in this plan won't work for your area, reply in the thread or DM me before Friday. I'd rather adjust it now than after people get used to it.

Thanks to @Grace Liu and <@U08STU987> for helping put this together.

input:
Summary of the Larkspan Freight escalation for @Ethan Wolfe and the account team.

background: Larkspan is one of our biggest customers on the enterprise plan, they process around 60,000 shipping labels a day through our API. since last tuesday they have been seeing intermittent timeouts on the `/v2/labels` endpoint, mostly between 9am and 11am eastern which is there peak time. their ops lead emailed support three times before it got escalated to us, which is a problem on it's own.

what we found:
- the timeouts are caused by a lock contention in the rate limiter. when a single tenant send a large burst of requests the limiter serialize them, and requests start queuing behind each other
- this only effects tenants with very high volume, so Larkspan and maybe two other customers
- it isnt related to the database upgrade last week even though the timing look suspicious

what we done so far:
- raised Larkspan's burst limit as a temporary workaround on friday, timeouts dropped by about 90% since then
- opened a fix to make the limiter per-shard instead of global, its in review https://example.com/pr/1187

next steps:
- ship the fix by wednesday after load testing in staging
- send Larkspan a written summary and timeline, Ethan can you own that?
- review why the support tickets took four days to reach engineering, i will set up a short meeting with the support leads

overall the customer is frustrated but not threatening to leave. they mostly want to know it wont happen again during their holiday peak in december.
expected:
Here is a summary of the Larkspan Freight escalation for @Ethan Wolfe and the account team.

Background: Larkspan is one of our biggest customers on the enterprise plan, and they process around 60,000 shipping labels a day through our API. Since last Tuesday, they have been seeing intermittent timeouts on the `/v2/labels` endpoint, mostly between 9 AM and 11 AM Eastern, which is their peak time. Their operations lead emailed support three times before the issue was escalated to us, which is a problem on its own.

What we found:
- The timeouts are caused by lock contention in the rate limiter. When a single tenant sends a large burst of requests, the limiter serializes them, and requests start queuing behind each other
- This only affects tenants with very high volume, so Larkspan and maybe two other customers
- It isn't related to the database upgrade last week, even though the timing looks suspicious

What we have done so far:
- Raised Larkspan's burst limit as a temporary workaround on Friday. Timeouts have dropped by about 90% since then
- Opened a fix to make the limiter per-shard instead of global. It's in review: https://example.com/pr/1187

Next steps:
- Ship the fix by Wednesday after load testing in staging
- Send Larkspan a written summary and timeline. Ethan, can you own that?
- Review why the support tickets took four days to reach engineering. I will set up a short meeting with the support leads

Overall, the customer is frustrated but not threatening to leave. They mostly want to know that it won't happen again during their holiday peak in December.

What went well:
- We hit the main goal: the pipeline now processes the full daily load in under 2 hours, down from almost 7
- Pairing between the backend and analytics folks worked really well, with less back-and-forth on requirements
- The staging environment was finally close enough to production that we caught most bugs before release

What didn't go well:
- The scope grew a lot in the middle of the project. We added the partner data feed in week 5, and it took nearly a month by itself
- Documentation was left until the end and is still incomplete, so new people on the team had a hard time getting started
- We had two releases that needed a rollback because the schema changes weren't backward compatible

Action items:
- Any new data source added after kickoff needs to go through a quick review with @Hannah Ortiz before we commit to it
- Write docs as we go: every PR that adds a new stage should update `docs/pipeline.md`
- Add a schema compatibility check to CI. Marco already has a prototype
- Schedule a mid-project check-in at week 4 to review scope and timeline

Thanks, everyone, for the honest discussion. It was one of the more useful retros we've had this year. The full board is here if you want to add anything: https://example.com/retro/q3-pipeline. I will close it on Friday.

@Leo Martins, here is the summary you asked for before tomorrow's architecture review.

The goal is to replace the polling loop in the notification service with an event-driven design. Today, each worker queries the database every five seconds for new notifications. At the current volume, that adds up to about 1.2 million queries per day, and most of them return nothing.

The proposal has three parts:
- The API writes a message to the event queue whenever a notification is created.
- Workers subscribe to the queue and process messages as they arrive.
- A small reconciliation job runs every hour to catch anything the queue missed.

Here is the configuration we tested in staging:
```
queue:
  name: notifications
  max_retries: 5
  visibility_timeout: 30s
```

In our tests, the median delivery time dropped from 2.6 seconds to 180 milliseconds, and database load fell by roughly 70%. We did not see any lost messages during a three-day soak test.

There are two open questions. First, we need to decide whether the reconciliation job should live in the same service or run separately. Second, the queue adds a new dependency, so the on-call runbook will need to be updated.

The full design document is at https://example.com/rfc/notifications-events, and the prototype is on the `events-prototype` branch. Please share any feedback in #architecture before the review.
